talks.title: HIdden Dangers of AI in Devloper Workflows
talks.teaser: Dwayne McDaniel Sr. investigates HIdden Dangers of AI in Devloper Workflows.
talks.summary:
Overview: Dwayne McDaniel presents at CornCon-X on hidden dangers of AI in developer workflows, focusing on human factors rather than technical jailbreaks or prompt injection.

Key Topics: AI tools enabling developers to act without thinking; the Butlerian Jihad concept of increasing actions without cognition; risks of over-reliance on AI-assisted development; and why human judgment remains essential.

Technical Details: McDaniel draws on Frank Herbert's Dune reference about machines increasing actions done without thinking, arguing AI coding assistants create similar risks where developers ship code they don't fully understand.

Takeaways: AI development tools risk degrading developer critical thinking. Teams should maintain code comprehension standards and resist shipping AI-generated code without human review and understanding.

talks.title: The SaaS and The Furious
talks.teaser: Ryan Wisniewski details The SaaS and The Furious.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Ryan Wisniewski, Threat Operations Lead at Obsidian Security, examines the escalating surge of enterprise Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) compromises. Presenting at CornCon, Wisniewski debunks the misconception that SaaS threats are confined to traditional Business Email Compromise (BEC), demonstrating how attackers exploit the SaaS ecosystem to execute rapid reconnaissance, persistent access, and data exfiltration. Drawing on telemetry from hundreds of real-world enterprise breaches, he outlines prevalent attacker kill chains, identity abuse techniques, and essential detection strategies.

Key Topics:
- SaaS compromise landscape and the collapse of traditional network perimeters
- Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing and non-human identity / OAuth sprawl
- Persistence via rogue MFA registration and defense evasion via inbox rules
- Rapid data exfiltration mechanics and helpdesk social engineering kill chains

Technical Details:
Wisniewski tracks over 220 publicly disclosed enterprise SaaS breaches, highlighting that modern attackers rarely rely on zero-day API exploits against platforms like Salesforce, Microsoft 365, or Workday. Instead, approximately 90% of compromises stem directly from identity compromise. A major unmanaged attack surface is non-human identity and OAuth application sprawl: the average enterprise tenant contains roughly 1,000 OAuth application grants, with over 90% remaining inactive for more than 90 days, providing unmonitored backdoors into corporate data. Attackers gain initial access primarily through Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) reverse proxy phishing, which intercepts session tokens and bypasses traditional multi-factor authentication (MFA), often targeting unmanaged employee mobile devices lacking Mobile Device Management (MDM).

Once inside, attackers establish persistence in approximately 85% of investigated cases by registering their own rogue software-based MFA device (such as an Okta Verify or Microsoft Authenticator instance) within the compromised user profile. Because identity providers (IdPs) permit selecting the destination device for push notifications, attackers route future MFA prompts to their own hardware, completely bypassing the legitimate employee. For defense evasion, adversaries create targeted email forwarding and mailbox rules. Rather than deleting notifications or marking them as read (which easily triggers basic alert rules), attackers program rules to divert login alerts, password resets, and payroll correspondence into default system folders that users rarely monitor, such as RSS Subscriptions or Conversation History.

During the discovery phase, attackers systematically browse single sign-on (SSO) app tiles to enumerate enterprise permissions, often utilizing stolen session tokens concurrently from multiple geographical IP addresses and user agents. Native SaaS search, export, and sharing capabilities facilitate rapid data exfiltration; in one documented financial sector breach, an attacker compromised an executive account and simply updated top-level OneDrive permissions to "share publicly," allowing unauthorized bulk downloads via external guest accounts. Wisniewski observes that the elapsed time between initial access and complete enterprise data exfiltration has dropped to as little as nine minutes. Furthermore, attackers actively abuse Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR) workflows combined with telecommunication SIM-swapping, as well as social engineering IT helpdesks using copycat MGM-style vishing techniques.

Key Takeaways:
Enterprises must shift detection focus from network perimeters to identity and SaaS telemetry, establishing continuous monitoring for rogue MFA device registrations and anomalous session token reuse across disparate geographic locations. Organizations must conduct automated audits of dormant OAuth integrations and revoke unutilized third-party permissions. Migrating away from SMS-based OTP toward FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware tokens and enforcing device compliance via MDM effectively mitigates AiTM reverse-proxy phishing and SIM-swapping attacks.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Alarmed & Dangerous: Exploiting Vulns in EMS Systems, McKeegan Curran, TAPS Team, Caterpillar
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Alarmed & Dangerous: Exploiting Vulns in EMS Systems, McKeegan Curran, TAPS Team, Caterpillar.
talks.summary:
Discovery via a Fraternity Fire Panel

Keegan Curran found a critical IDOR while proxying his fraternity's upgraded fire-alarm mobile app with Fiddler. Changing the site-number parameter in API calls returned other customers' data within minutes, despite the app's outdated codebase and infrequent security updates.

Exposed Sensitive Data

Vulnerable responses leaked customer addresses, lockbox combinations, and digital-lock codes for fire and security systems. Because POST, PUT, and DELETE were equally affected, attackers could modify—not just view—remote system state without authentication beyond a valid app session.

Abuse Scenarios at Scale

Curran mapped roughly 597 vulnerable sites in Davenport, over 14,000 in Iowa, and 269,000 across North America including hospitals, schools, power plants, and Fortune 50 facilities. Attackers could trigger immediate emergency dispatch, place alarms in test mode to suppress real events, or induce alarm fatigue before physical intrusion.

Remediation Timeline

Reported in July 2024 through a local intermediary because the vendor lacked a formal bug-bounty program, the vendor patched quickly given the potential for mass false dispatches and critical-infrastructure impact. The talk underscores how overlooked physical-security SaaS APIs can threaten public safety.

talks.title: An alternate ending to Star Wars and how you mitigate risk, John Aron, CEO, Aronetics
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of An alternate ending to Star Wars and how you mitigate risk, John Aron, CEO, Aronetics.
talks.summary:
Star Wars as risk metaphor

John Aron, CEO of Aronetics and adviser to the Joint Applied Task Force supporting USSOCOM, uses Star Wars imagery to discuss federal cyber risk mitigation. He blends personal near-death experience, Equifax-scale breach context, and skepticism toward vendor hype about trillion-dollar cyber "opportunities" while major hacks continue.

Identity and breach reality

Aron argues consumers maintain plural online identities yet cannot trust breached credit bureaus to protect them. He frames cyber defense as navigating fog-of-war, citing FBI guidance that defenders face two categories of organizations: those hacked and those that do not yet know it.

Defense in depth via fighters

He maps X-Wing layered defenses versus agile TIE fighters—speed and maneuverability without implicit channel security—to different mitigation strategies. Open-source intelligence revealing the Death Star exhaust-port flaw illustrates how adversaries find single points of failure when layered controls are bypassed.
